lessons.title: Science Takes Flight

activities.prompt: How can curiosity help us learn to fly?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Science Is Everywhere
activities.body: Science covers everything, from tiny objects to distant stars. A science book invites you to ask questions, perform experiments and explore. You might look at cells inside a leaf or study the sun and stars. Curiosity helps learning take flight. A simple paper plane inspired real scientific explorations of flight. Early inventors studied bird wings while modern engineers designed aircraft.

Questions and experiments help you explore.
Curiosity can make learning take flight.

activities.explanation: Curiosity leads the way when learning takes flight.

lessons.title: Thinking Like a Scientist

activities.prompt: How can curiosity help us discover answers and solve real-world challenges?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What scientists do
activities.body: Scientific thinking starts with curiosity and asks questions. It welcomes the unknown and asks how things work. It also asks why events happen. Scientists learn through activities and experiments. Useful experiences become stepping stones to deeper understanding. Science connects with society, and different fields can inspire each other.
keyPoints: Ask questions and welcome curiosity.
Learn through activities and experiments.
Connect science with society and other fields.
activities.explanation: Scientific thinking helps you explore questions and learn about the world.

activities.prompt: Which action best shows scientific thinking?
options: asking questions and accepting the unknown
assuming how things work without asking why
activities.explanation: Scientific thinking welcomes curiosity, asks questions, and accepts the unknown.

activities.prompt: Scientific thinking accepts that some answers are not known yet.
activities.explanation: Scientific thinking is open to the unknown. It welcomes curiosity and asks questions.

activities.prompt: Scientists ask ______ things work and why events happen.
activities.hint: This asks about the way something works.
activities.explanation: Scientists ask how things work and why events happen.

activities.prompt: Match each science idea with its connection.
activities.explanation: These connections show how scientific thinking links ideas, activities, society, and nature.

activities.prompt: Put these ideas in the learning sequence.
activities.explanation: Activities and experiments help us learn. Useful experiences then become stepping stones to deeper understanding.

activities.prompt: How can scientific ideas in one area lead to discoveries in another?
activities.explanation: Different science fields are interconnected. Scientific ideas can inspire discoveries in another area.

activities.prompt: Science can help us address environmental challenges.
activities.explanation: Science is connected to society. It can help us address environmental challenges.

activities.prompt: Your class learns that human activities are linked to nature changes. What should it ask next?
options: Ask how and why changes happen
Assume the natural world stays unchanged
Keep science fields separate from one another
activities.explanation: Human activities are linked to changes in the natural world. Scientists ask how and why changes happen.

lessons.title: Materials and Their Changes

activities.prompt: Why are some fruits sour, and what happens when haldi stains are washed?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Materials Around Us
activities.body: Materials have properties we can examine. It asks why some fruits are sour. It asks what happens when a haldi stain is washed. We will meet metals and non-metals. Some changes can reverse, while others cannot. Heating can speed up some changes. Batteries, lamps and wires help us investigate materials. The Sun’s heat makes water evaporate from seas. Water falls as rain and may trickle down into ground.
keyPoints: Materials can be grouped by their properties.
Some changes can be reversed, while others cannot.
Heating can make some changes happen faster.
A torch battery eventually runs out.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects material properties, changes, investigations and water.

activities.explanation: Yes. The lesson says we can classify materials by their properties.

lessons.title: Living Things, Time and Shadows

activities.prompt: How do shadows help us understand how living things grow and change over time?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Living Things Change
activities.body: Animals need food and breathing to grow. Blood carries nutrients from food throughout the body. Plants also need food, and may breathe differently from animals. Bodies change as they grow, and can change rapidly during middle-school years. Life on Earth has evolved over a long period. A wall clock or wristwatch shows time passing. Early humans used the Sun’s shadows to tell time.
keyPoints: Living things need food to grow.
Bodies change during growth.
Clocks and shadows can show time.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect growth, survival and the passing of time.

activities.title: Bodies During Growth
activities.prompt: What happens to our bodies as we grow?
activities.explanation: Our bodies change as we grow, so change is the correct answer.

activities.title: Animal Growth Needs
activities.prompt: Animals need to eat and breathe in order to grow.
activities.explanation: Animals need both food and breathing to grow.

activities.title: Blood’s Important Job
activities.prompt: Blood carries ______ from food throughout the body.
activities.hint: These parts of food travel around your body.
activities.explanation: Blood carries nutrients from food to every part of the body.

activities.title: Early Time Clues
activities.prompt: Why did early humans use the Sun’s shadows?
activities.explanation: Early humans used the Sun’s shadows to tell the time.

activities.title: Time and Change
activities.body: A wall clock or wristwatch tells us the time and how it passes. Early humans used the Sun’s shadows to tell the time. Living things also change over time. Our bodies change as we grow, and rapidly during middle-school years. Life on Earth has evolved over a long period. These changes happen over time.
keyPoints: Clocks show time passing.
Sun shadows helped tell time.
Growth and evolution show change.
activities.explanation: Clocks and shadows show time, while growth and evolution show change.

activities.title: Match the Clues
activities.prompt: Match each clue with what it tells us.

activities.explanation: Sun shadows and clocks tell time. The other pairs show needs, growth and evolution.

activities.title: Different Ways to Breathe
activities.prompt: Plants may breathe in a way that is different from animals.
activities.explanation: The lesson says plants may breathe differently from animals.

Animals need food and breathing; clocks changed animal bodies.
Animals need food and breathing; shadows replaced animal food.
Animals need food and breathing; shadows helped people tell time.
activities.explanation: Animals need food and breathing to grow. Early humans used the Sun’s shadows to tell time.

activities.prompt: How does light help us explore space and understand the world around us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Light and Science
activities.body: People have developed many ways to generate light. Studying light helps us understand the universe. The Earth and Moon can both cast shadows, and their shadows can lead to eclipses. Day and night depend on light from the Sun. The Earth rotates around its axis, while the Moon goes around the Earth. The chapters use observations, questions and experiments to build your knowledge. Experiments may also create new questions.

The Earth and Moon can cast shadows.
Observations and experiments build knowledge.
Experiments can create new questions.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects light, space and scientific exploration.

activities.title: Questions and Answers
activities.body: In school and tests, we usually receive questions and are expected to answer them. Finding answers matters, but asking interesting questions matters too. Great scientists ask questions and answer them.

lessons.title: Litmus and the Nature of Substances

activities.prompt: Could a tiny splash reveal whether a substance is acidic or basic?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Litmus Shows Us
activities.body: Litmus is a natural substance obtained from lichens. Litmus paper is available in blue and red colours. It shows different colours in acidic or basic substances. Blue litmus paper turns red in acid. Red litmus paper turns blue in a base. This colour change makes litmus an acid-base indicator.
keyPoints: Litmus is obtained from lichens.
Blue and red litmus paper are available.
Different colours show acidic and basic substances.
Litmus is an acid-base indicator.
activities.explanation: Litmus helps us recognise some substances by their colour changes.

activities.prompt: The litmus activity should use red litmus paper as well as blue.

activities.title: Why Use Litmus?
activities.prompt: Why is litmus called an acid-base indicator?
activities.explanation: Litmus shows different colours, so it acts as an acid-base indicator.

Hot water is poured over crushed rose petals.
Red rose extract can test acidic, basic and neutral substances.

lessons.title: Mixing Acids and Bases

activities.prompt: What happens when lemon juice meets lime water?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Mixing Acids and Bases
activities.body: Lemon juice is diluted with about twenty drops of water. A drop of blue litmus solution is added, and the solution turns red. Lime water is then added slowly while the solution is swirled. The colour changes from red to blue. The solution is no longer acidic because lime water has neutralised the acid's effect. This is called a neutralisation reaction. Salt and water form while heat is released.
keyPoints: Blue litmus solution turns red in diluted lemon juice.
Lime water neutralises the effect of the acid.
Salt and water form while heat is released.
activities.explanation: You can spot the reaction through its colour changes.

Letting air out can return the balloon to its earlier state. Water can also change between solid, liquid and gas. These changes affect physical properties such as shape, size and state.

The material stays the same during a physical change.
Shape, size and state are physical properties.

activities.title: Changes Can Be Useful or Harmful
activities.body: Some changes are useful, while others are harmful in a particular situation. A change may be useful or harmful, depending on the situation. activities.title: Growing Through Life
activities.body: People pass through infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood and old age. Each person passes through these stages at a different pace. Adolescence comes between childhood and adulthood. It is a period of rapid growth and development between ages 10 and 19. During this time, the body prepares for adulthood. Height changes become more noticeable. Adolescent boys may get a hoarse voice. Both boys and girls grow hair in different body parts.

Adolescence is rapid growth and development between ages 10 and 19.
During adolescence, the body prepares for adulthood.

activities.prompt: Why can two places feel so different in the same winter?

activities.title: Heat Around Us
activities.body: The Sun is the main source of heat and light for us on Earth. Kerala is nearer the equator than Sikkim. The climate near the equator is generally hot. Heat moves from hotter parts to colder parts by conduction. A heated particle passes heat to its neighbour. Particles keep their positions. Heat mainly travels by conduction in solids. Metals conduct heat well, so they are used for cooking utensils.
keyPoints: Heat moves from hotter to colder parts.
A heated particle passes heat to its neighbour.
Particles stay in their positions.
activities.explanation: You have learnt how heat travels through solids.

activities.explanation: Conduction moves heat from a hotter part of an object to a colder part.

activities.title: Heat, Conductors and Insulators

Air also slows heat moving through it. Woollen fabric traps air, and layers of blankets trap air too. Trapped air reduces heat loss. Hollow bricks trap air. Wood-and-mud layers prevent heat loss and keep houses warm.

Glass, wood and trapped air slow heat transfer.
Air is trapped in fabrics, blankets and hollow bricks.
Wood and mud layers reduce heat loss.

activities.prompt: What secrets hide in the way air and water move?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How heat moves
activities.body: Smoke contains hot gases and tiny solid pieces called particles. Air around a candle becomes heated. Air in a cup expands, becomes lighter and rises. The cup rises. Heated water expands, becomes lighter and rises. Cooler water comes down to replace it. This movement of particles transfers heat and is called convection. At night, cooler air moves from land to sea, making a land breeze.
keyPoints: Smoke contains hot gases and tiny solid pieces called particles.
Heated air and water expand, become lighter and rise.
Convection transfers heat through moving particles.
At night, cooler air moves from land to sea.
activities.explanation: Convection transfers heat through the movement of particles.

activities.prompt: Warmed air becomes lighter and rises.

activities.title: How Time Was Measured

activities.title: How a Pendulum Moves
activities.body: A simple pendulum has a heavy ball called the bob. The bob hangs from a rigid support by a long thread. When it swings, the bob repeats its path after a fixed interval. This motion is periodic. One oscillation is completed when the bob moves from an extreme position and returns. The time taken for one oscillation is called the time period.

One oscillation ends when the bob returns.
The time period measures one complete oscillation.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Food and Digestion Begin

activities.prompt: What happens to your food as it travels through your body?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Food and Digestion
activities.body: Animals get energy from the food they eat. Food contains complex parts called carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Digestion means breaking these parts into simpler forms. It starts in your mouth and ends at the anus. It happens inside the alimentary canal, a long tube in your body. Mechanical digestion is the first breakdown of food. Teeth crush and chew food into fine pieces.
keyPoints: Food gives animals energy.
Complex food parts break into simpler forms.
Digestion starts in the mouth and ends at the anus.
The alimentary canal is a long tube inside the body.
Teeth crush and chew food into fine pieces.
activities.explanation: Digestion breaks complex food parts into simpler forms.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Food Passes Through the Oesophagus and Stomach

activities.prompt: How does your food travel from your mouth to your stomach?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Food Moves Through Your Body
activities.body: Your food travels through a tube from your mouth to your stomach. This tube is called the oesophagus, or food pipe. The tongue mixes chewed food with saliva and pushes it onwards. The pipe walls contract and relax in waves. These movements push food into the stomach. The stomach churns food and releases juice, acid and mucus. The juice breaks proteins into simpler parts. Acid kills many harmful bacteria, while mucus protects the stomach lining. The stomach changes partly digested food into a semi-liquid mass. The small intestine is almost 6 metres long. It is also the longest part of the alimentary canal.
keyPoints: The oesophagus carries food from the mouth to the stomach.
The stomach churns food and helps break down proteins.
Mucus protects the stomach lining from acid.
activities.explanation: This card shows how food moves and is protected inside your body.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Absorption, Waste Removal and Other Digestive Systems

activities.prompt: What happens to the food we eat after it leaves the stomach?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How the Body Uses Food
activities.body: Absorption means taking nutrients into the blood. The small intestine receives digestive secretions from three sources. Bile neutralises acids. Pancreatic juice is basic and breaks down carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Digestive juice further breaks down partly digested food. Thousands of finger-like projections help nutrient absorption. The large intestine absorbs water and some salts. Egestion means removing solid waste from the body. Ruminants and birds use special methods for food breakdown.
keyPoints: Absorption moves digested nutrients into the blood.
The large intestine absorbs water and some salts.
Egestion removes solid waste from the body.
activities.explanation: These points connect digestion, absorption and waste removal.

activities.title: How humans breathe
activities.body: Breathing is the process of inhaling and exhaling air. When you inhale, you take in oxygen. When you exhale, you release carbon dioxide. Air enters through your nostrils and moves through nasal passages. Tiny hair and mucus trap dust and dirt. The passages branch and end in tiny balloon-like sacs called alveoli. Your respiratory system helps your body breathe. The rib cage protects your lungs.

Nostrils and nasal passages lead towards tiny alveoli, while the rib cage protects the lungs.

lessons.title: Transport in Plants

activities.prompt: How does water travel all the way up a tall plant?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Plants Get Water and Food
activities.body: All living beings need water to grow. Roots take in water and minerals from soil. Minerals are important nutrients for plant growth. Plants use water during photosynthesis, the process in which plants use water. Xylem is a thin tube-like structure in plants. Phloem is a set of thin tube-like structures. Food made in leaves is carried to all parts of a plant.
keyPoints: Roots take in water and minerals from soil.
Plants use water during photosynthesis.
Phloem carries food made in leaves to all plant parts.
activities.explanation: Plants take in water and minerals, and transport food to their parts.

activities.prompt: What do roots take in from the soil?
activities.explanation: Roots take in water and minerals from the soil. These help the plant grow.

activities.prompt: Plants need water to grow.
activities.explanation: Yes, all living beings need water to grow. Plants are living beings.

activities.prompt: Match each word with its correct description.
pairs: take in water and minerals from soil
are important nutrients for plant growth
has a few drops of red ink added
is a set of thin tube-like structures
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a part or thing with the description given in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Which structure carries food made in leaves?
activities.explanation: Phloem is a set of thin tube-like structures that carries food.

activities.prompt: Xylem is a thin tube-like ______ found in plants.
activities.hint: It is the tube-like part described in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Xylem is called a thin tube-like structure found in plants.

activities.prompt: Phloem carries water from the soil.
activities.explanation: Phloem carries food. Roots take in water from the soil.

activities.prompt: If roots cannot take in water and minerals, which needs of the plant may be affected?
options: Red ink and food for growth
activities.explanation: Water is needed for growth, and minerals are important nutrients for plant growth.

activities.prompt: Put these plant steps in order.
items: Roots take in water and minerals from soil
Phloem carries food to all parts of a plant
activities.explanation: Roots take in materials first. Plants use water, make food in leaves, and carry it through phloem.

lessons.title: Respiration in Plants

activities.prompt: How do plants breathe without lungs?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Plants Respire
activities.body: Plants respire, just like other living beings. During respiration, glucose is broken down in the presence of oxygen. This releases energy, which helps plants grow and develop. Every part of a plant respires, whether it is green or non-green. In an experiment, moong bean seeds are soaked overnight and kept in the dark. Germinating seeds produce extra carbon dioxide. The lime water may turn milky in both test tubes.
keyPoints: Plants respire like all living beings.
Respiration breaks down glucose using oxygen and releases energy.
Every part of a plant respires, even non-green parts.
activities.explanation: Respiration gives plants energy for growth and development.

activities.title: Who Respires?
activities.prompt: Which statement is true about living beings and plants?
options: All living beings, including plants, respire.
activities.explanation: All living beings respire. Every part of a plant does this too.

activities.prompt: Moong bean seeds are soaked in water overnight.
activities.explanation: The moong bean seeds are soaked in water before they are left undisturbed.

activities.prompt: During respiration, glucose is broken down in the presence of ______.
activities.hint: Name the gas used during respiration.
activities.explanation: Respiration breaks down glucose when oxygen is present.

activities.title: Prepare the Experiment
activities.prompt: Match each material with its preparation.
activities.explanation: These preparations help show the effects of respiration in germinating seeds.

activities.title: What May Happen?
activities.prompt: What may happen in both test tubes?
options: The lime water may turn milky.
activities.explanation: The lime water may turn milky in both test tubes.

activities.title: Why Is Extra Carbon Dioxide Produced?
activities.prompt: Why do germinating seeds produce additional carbon dioxide?
activities.explanation: Germinating seeds respire, so they produce additional carbon dioxide.

activities.title: Respiration and Plant Growth
activities.prompt: Put these ideas in order during plant respiration.

The energy helps plants grow and develop
activities.explanation: Respiration breaks down glucose, releases energy, and supports plant growth.

activities.prompt: Only green parts of a plant respire.
activities.explanation: Every part of a plant respires, whether it is green or non-green.

lessons.title: Light Sources and Luminous Objects

activities.prompt: Why do fireflies glow, and why does the Moon shine at night?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Objects that make their own light
activities.body: Luminous objects give out their own light. These include the Sun, stars, lightning, natural fire and some animals. Non-luminous objects do not. The Moon reflects sunlight, so it is non-luminous. The Sun is Earth's main natural light source. Human-made lighting began with fire. Later, people used animal fat, oil, wax and gas. Electric lighting now meets most lighting needs. LED lamps use less power, shine brighter and last longer.
keyPoints: Luminous objects give out their own light.
The Moon reflects sunlight instead of making its own light.
Fire and electric lighting are human-made light sources.
activities.explanation: Luminous means giving out your own light rather than reflecting it.

activities.prompt: What does the Moon do with sunlight that falls on it?
options: It gives out its own light.
activities.explanation: The Moon is non-luminous because it reflects sunlight that falls on it.

activities.prompt: The Moon gives out its own light.
activities.explanation: The Moon is non-luminous because it reflects sunlight that falls on it.

activities.prompt: Match each object with its correct description.

Reflects sunlight that falls on it
activities.explanation: Each matching pair shows how its light source works.

activities.title: Fireflies and human-made light
activities.body: Fireflies are seasonal insects that use light to communicate. Their numbers are decreasing. One reason for this is light pollution. Human-made lighting began when humans first created fire. People later used animal fat, oil, wax and gas to make fire. Electric lighting now meets most people's lighting needs.
keyPoints: Fireflies use light to communicate.
Light pollution is one reason fireflies are decreasing.
People first used fire for human-made lighting.
activities.explanation: Fireflies show how living things can use light for communication.

activities.prompt: LED lamps use less ______, shine brighter and last longer than traditional lamps.

activities.explanation: LED lamps use less power than traditional lamps.

activities.explanation: Light pollution is one reason for the decreasing number of fireflies.

activities.prompt: Which statement about these light sources is correct?

lessons.title: Light Travels in a Straight Line

activities.prompt: Can we make light reveal the path it takes?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How light travels
activities.body: Light travels in a straight line. You can test this with three matchboxes, three holes, a torch and a screen. When the holes are in one line and at the same height, the torch lamp gives a bright spot on the screen. If the holes are not in one line, no light spot appears. A candle flame is visible through a straight pipe, but not a bent pipe.
keyPoints: Light travels in a straight line.
Holes must be in one line at the same height.
A candle flame is visible through a straight pipe.
activities.explanation: These observations help you see that light follows a straight path.

activities.prompt: Light travels in a straight line.
activities.explanation: The matchbox observations show that light travels in a straight line.

activities.prompt: Which setup should you use to receive a bright spot on the screen?
options: Three holes in one line, with the torch at their height.
Three holes at different heights, with the torch nearby.
Three holes in a bent line, with the torch at their height.
activities.explanation: Keep the three holes in one line at the same height as the torch lamp. This setup makes the screen receive a bright spot.

activities.prompt: When the three holes are not in one line, the screen does not show a light ______.
activities.hint: This bright mark appears when the setup is correct.
activities.explanation: The screen does not show the light spot when the holes are not in line.

activities.prompt: Match each observation with its result.
pairs: A bright spot on the screen
No light spot on the screen
The holes are not in one line
activities.explanation: Each result follows from the straight-line test in your book.

activities.prompt: Put the investigation steps and result in order.
items: Arrange the three matchboxes in a straight line
Keep all three holes at the same height
Place the torch lamp at the same height
The screen receives a bright spot
activities.explanation: The boxes, holes and torch are aligned before the bright spot appears.

activities.prompt: Which pipe lets you see a candle flame?
activities.explanation: A candle flame can be seen through a straight pipe. It cannot be seen through a bent pipe.

activities.prompt: The bent-pipe test shows that light travels in a straight line.
activities.explanation: A candle flame cannot be seen through a bent pipe. The bent-pipe test also shows that light travels in a straight line.

activities.prompt: Which statement about light is correct?
options: A laser beam in water can be seen on a straight path.
A candle flame can be seen through a bent pipe.
activities.explanation: A laser beam in water follows a straight path. Light can sometimes bend around corners, but this is studied in higher grades.

lessons.title: Light through Materials and Shadow Formation

activities.prompt: What happens to light when it meets different materials?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Materials Make Shadows
activities.body: Transparent materials let light pass almost completely through. Translucent materials let light pass partly through. Opaque materials stop light. An opaque object blocks light and creates a dark patch called a shadow. A shadow needs a light source, an opaque object and a screen. Shape, size and sharpness depend on the object's position. Opaque objects make darker shadows; translucent objects make lighter shadows. Some transparent objects create faint shadows.
keyPoints: Transparent materials let light pass almost completely.
Translucent materials let light pass partly.
An opaque object in light's path creates a shadow.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you work out how different materials make shadows.

activities.title: Change a shadow

tasks.say: Move the object close to the lamp.
tasks.then: The shadow grows large.

tasks.say: Move it far from the lamp.
tasks.then: The shadow shrinks towards the size of the object.

activities.takeaway: Light travels in straight lines, and an object blocks it to make a shadow.
activities.explanation: Light travels in straight lines, and an object blocks it to make a shadow.

activities.prompt: Which type of material lets light pass almost completely through?
activities.explanation: Transparent materials let light pass almost completely through them.

activities.prompt: Translucent materials let light pass partly through them.
activities.explanation: Light passes partly through translucent materials.

activities.prompt: Match each material to what happens to light.
pairs: Light passes almost completely through it
Light does not pass through it
activities.explanation: Transparent and translucent materials pass different amounts of light. Opaque materials stop light.

activities.prompt: The dark patch where light does not reach is called a ______.
activities.hint: It forms behind an opaque object.
activities.explanation: This dark patch is called a shadow.

activities.prompt: Which one is given as an example of a shadow screen?
activities.explanation: Walls, floors, ground and other surfaces can act as screens.

activities.prompt: Put the shadow-forming events in order.
items: The opaque object blocks the light.
A dark patch forms on the screen.
activities.explanation: The opaque object blocks light. The dark patch then forms on the screen.

activities.prompt: Changing an opaque object's colour changes the colour of its shadow.
activities.explanation: Changing an opaque object's colour does not change the colour of its shadow.

activities.prompt: Which object forms a darker shadow?
activities.explanation: Opaque objects form darker shadows. Translucent objects make lighter shadows. Some transparent objects create faint shadows.

lessons.title: Reflection of Light and Plane Mirrors

activities.prompt: What can we learn about light by watching our reflections?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Light and Plane Mirrors
activities.body: Light travels in a straight line. When it meets a shiny surface or mirror, its direction changes. This is reflection. A plane mirror makes an image that is erect, the same size as its object, and cannot be obtained on a screen. Stand close to a mirror, and its image appears close. Stand far away, and it appears far away. Left and right appear reversed. This is lateral inversion.
keyPoints: A shiny surface changes the direction of light.
A plane mirror forms an erect image of the same size.
Left and right appear reversed in a mirror image.
activities.explanation: A shiny surface changes light's direction, and a plane mirror forms an erect image.

activities.title: Bounce light off a mirror

tasks.say: Make the ray come in at 60 degrees.
tasks.then: It leaves at 60 degrees too.

tasks.say: Shine it straight down the normal.
tasks.then: It comes straight back.

activities.takeaway: The angle going out always equals the angle coming in.
activities.explanation: The angle going out always equals the angle coming in.

activities.title: Light Meets a Mirror

activities.explanation: A plane mirror forms an erect image. That image is the same size as its object.

activities.title: How a Pinhole Camera Works
activities.body: A pinhole camera forms an image when light rays pass through a tiny hole. Two cardboard boxes slide together. Make a small hole in the larger box's opposite face. Use thin paper that lets light through as the screen, facing inside. Cover your head and camera with a dark cloth. Move the smaller box until an image appears. The image is upside-down.

Thin translucent paper is the screen.
The image is upside-down.
activities.explanation: You can make a simple camera that forms an upside-down image.

activities.title: The Small Opening

Turning it gives a different pattern each time.

Reflection helps you see objects that are not directly visible.
A kaleidoscope makes changing patterns using three mirror strips.

lessons.title: How the Earth Rotates

activities.prompt: Why does the Sun seem to move across the sky?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The spinning Earth
activities.body: The Earth turns around itself. This turning is called rotation. Because of this turning, the Sun seems to move. You see the Sun rise in the East and set in the West. The Earth’s axis of rotation is an imaginary line through its North Pole and South Pole. One rotation takes about 24 hours.
keyPoints: The Earth turns around itself.
The Sun rises in the East and sets in the West.
The axis is an imaginary line through both poles.

activities.title: When Earth’s Shadow Covers the Moon
